name: Faire Atta
confidence_why: No description of Faire Atta stress exists: the only first-hand material is unpublished SIL wordlists (Nickell 1981; SIL c. 1970) whose sporadic accent marks fall on the penult in some words and on the final syllable in others, while the one published analysis of any Atta variety, Whittle & Lusted (1963), describes Pamplona Atta (final primary stress, with long vowels carrying a pitch rise that sounds like stress), so any rule stated for Faire Atta would be an inference rather than a report.

new_statements.quote: A word is bordered by word juncture (which is characterized by potential pause) and marked by primary stress on the ultima. Word juncture is represented by space. Primary stress is characterized by volume, usually on the lowest pitch level of the speaker, but varying with the type of intonation contour. It is perhaps best described as a low push. Secondary stress accompanied by a rise in pitch occurs on long vowels. Because of its length and higher pitch characteristics, it sounds, to American ears hearing it for the first time, like primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Whittle, Claudia & Ruth Lusted. 1963. Interaction of coexistent phonemic systems in Atta (Northern Cagayan Negrito). In Elmer Wolfenden (ed.), Papers on Philippine Languages No. 1, 26-39. Manila: Institute for Language Teaching & Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.1, p. 28 (p. 3; page scan); dialect identification p. 26; vowel length p. 30; loanword stress sec. 3.6 pp. 37-38
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (lines 90-99) and the page scan printed p. 28, sec. 2.1). The passage 'A word is bordered by word juncture (which is characterized by potential pause) and marked by primary stress on the ultima. Word juncture is represented by space. Primary stress is characterized by volume, usually on the lowest pitch level of the speaker, but varying with the type of intonation contour. It is perhaps best described as a low push. Secondary stress accompanied by a rise in pitch occurs on long vowels. Because of its length and higher pitch characteristics, it sounds, to American ears hearing it for the first time, like primary stress.' is there word for word (only end-of-line hyphenation diff…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In (Pamplona) Atta every word carries primary stress (a low-pitched intensity 'push') on its final syllable; what sounds like non-final stress is analysed as contrastive vowel length, long vowels bearing a secondary stress with raised pitch (e.g. Spanish vaca > ba:ka). NOTE: this describes the Pamplona dialect (Pamplona Atta, pamp1244), the closest described relative; no statement exists for Faire Atta itself, whose 1981 SIL wordlist marks accents on both penults and finals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress, accompanied by a pitch rise, falls on long vowels (length contrastive for a, i, u; e and o always long); stressed vowels of Spanish loans are borrowed as long vowels with this secondary stress + high pitch (sec. 3.6).
new_statements.exceptions: None for primary stress (stated as always on the ultima); length restricted to the second vowel of a vowel cluster; e/o always long.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain = the word as bounded by potential pause (word juncture); primary stress interacts with intonation contour. Statement is for the Pamplona dialect of Atta (authors list Allacapan, Marag, Pamplona dialects; Faire/Santo Niño Atta is not among them and is a separate Glottolog language fair1238).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Whittle & Lusted 1963) describes the PAMPLONA dialect of Atta = Pamplona Atta, Glottolog pamp1244 / ISO att (authors: dialects Allacapan, Marag, Pamplona; paper treats Pamplona). Faire Atta (fair1238, azt; Santo Niño/Faire and Rizal, Cagayan) is a separate Glottolog language in the same Atta subgroup and has NO description beyond three SIL wordlists (Nickell 1981 Calassitan; SIL 1960-80 Bullakit; Nickell 1981 Annip, Rizal - the last possibly not Atta at all: SIL record says no ISO code, and the Calassitan sheet says Rizal speech is called 'Imalaweg', i.e. Malaweg/Itawis area). The Faire wordlist accents fall on both penults and finals, which under Whittle & Lusted's analysis would be long-vowel secondary stress vs. final primary stress, but no source says so for Faire Atta. The Whittle & Lusted PDF and PL C-22 were also copied to with a note, since the earlier scan marked that paper the named source could not be reached for pamp1244.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and renders of the handwritten SIL 77200 original). Header on p. 2 reads exactly 'LANGUAGE: Atta / PLACE: Annip, Rizal / LANGUAGE ASSISTANT: Liyaban Danaw / DATE: 7-24-81 / TECHNICIAN: Tom Nickell' with the margin note 'didn't understand Pamplona tape' (also '56 houses', 'Travel- Rizal, Sm., wife- from Iskalaw'). The twelve forms the compiler transcribed are on the page with the acute where stated: abaká, ngamín, napóray, sikád (written sikə́d), mapasíran, dúlay, sínay, dakál (dakə́l), dága?, malawág, mangúmma; the one minor difference is item 27, which the compiler read as 'maisú' but which the typed transcription (now obtained) renders 'ma:sú', i.e. a length colon plus final accent…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for fair1238. The only existing statement ('primary stress on the ultima', Whittle & Lusted 1963) is about Pamplona Atta. This list is the Annip (Rizal) variety, which SIL says has no ISO code and is 'reportedly 90% similar to Atta Faire'; its accent marks fall on the ultima OR the penult, so it does not on its face match a fixed-ultima rule, but it is a wordlist, not an analysis, and the penult marks may be the long/high-pitched vowels of the Pamplona analysis. Read as: first stress data for the Faire-area varieties, lexically placed accent on one of the last two syllables.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The document is a raw 372-item wordlist with no prose about stress. The compiler wrote an acute accent on one vowel of nearly every entry, and the marked syllable is the ultima in some words (abaká, ngamín, sikád, maisú, malawág) and the penult in others (napóray, dúlay, sínay, dága?, mangúmma), so stress placement is recorded as lexically distributed between the last two syllables, as in other Philippine languages. Whether the penult marks correspond to what Whittle & Lusted (Pamplona) treat as long vowels with secondary stress and high pitch cannot be decided from the list.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no statement of a rule at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (SIL 77200) is the Annip, Rizal variety: SIL says 'There is no iso 639-3 code for this language. It is reportedly 90% similar to Atta Faire', and the field sheet notes the consultant 'didn't understand Pamplona tape' and that the language is called 'Imalaweg' in Rizal. Work 1's open copy is Ilongot (Bugkalot), and Reid 1971's Atta entry is Pamplona Atta. Work 2 (SIL 77213) is catalogued under Pamplona Atta [att]. The existing statement (Whittle & Lusted 1963) is Pamplona Atta (pamp1244). Faire Atta proper is represented only by the on-disk SIL 77207 Calassitan, Faire typed list (not among the listed works), which shows the same accent-marked pattern.

readall_conflicts: The only prose statement on record (Whittle & Lusted 1963, 'primary stress on the ultima', with secondary stress and high pitch on long vowels) describes the Pamplona dialect, not Faire Atta. The only Faire-area data opened, Nickell's 1981 Annip (Rizal) wordlist, and the on-disk Calassitan, Faire list (SIL 77207, same compiler, same week) mark an acute on the ultima in some words and on the penult in others (Annip: abaká, sikád, malawág vs. napóray, dúlay, sínay; Calassitan: abaká, kagát, tumubbág vs. mapúray, sínay, mangúmma). Taken literally the lists disagree with a fixed-ultima rule; but they are field transcriptions with no analysis, from different varieties (the Annip consultant 'didn't understand Pamplona tape'), and the penult marks could be Whittle & Lusted's long vowels under a different notation. No source opened states a rule for Faire Atta itself.
